title: Spotlight

subtitle.text: "Hurry up, Tyler! My mom's waiting in the car." Matt Whitman gathered up his backpack and sleeping
bag. It was Saturday morning, and the two boys had just spent the night at their
friend Brian's house. "Great sleepover, Brian," Matt said. "That movie was the scariest one yet!" "It was
pretty good," Brian said. "Even I was frightened!" Tyler was still fumbling with his sleeping bag. "Well,
I wasn't scared at all." Brian grinned at Tyler. "No, you just happened to go into
the kitchen for more popcorn at the exact moment when those kids were walking into that haunted
house." "Okay, maybe I was a little scared," Tyler admitted. "But you should have seen your face
when that zombie jumped out of the bushes." They all laughed. Brian's phone buzzed. He frowned as
he quickly read the text message. Then he put the phone back in his pocket. "Who
was that?" Tyler asked. "Just Becky breaking up with me." "Didn't you two already break up twice
this week?" Matt said. "Yeah, but we got back together." "Apparently you forgot to tell her," Matt
said. Brian scowled at the joke, but Tyler laughed. Outside, Matt's mother honked the car horn.
"See you later, Brian." Matt opened the front door. Tyler followed Matt as he ran down the
walk and jumped into the back seat of the car. "Hi, guys," Mrs. Whitman said. "Did you
get any sleep last night?" "Of course not, Mom. No one sleeps at a sleepover." "Especially
when we're watching really scary movies," Tyler said. "Now you admit they were really scary," Matt teased
his friend as they drove away. "I thought you were just a little scared. Oh, wait a
minute. Weren't you the one hiding your face in your pillow when the monster grabbed those
kids? I thought you—" "My pillow! I forgot my pillow!" Tyler cried. "I couldn't find my backpack
this morning, so I took off the pillowcase to use as a sack. We have to go
back." Mrs. Whitman turned the car around and drove to Brian's house. Tyler ran in and
soon returned with his pillow and backpack. "Brian's mom found my backpack underneath a chair," he explained
happily as he buckled his seatbelt. "Are we all set now?" Mrs. Whitman turned on the car
radio. "Matt, it's almost time for your favorite program. They're doing Don Carlo today." Matt's eyes widened
in horror. He couldn't believe his mother had just said that in front of Tyler. "What's
wrong with you?" Tyler pointed at Matt. "You look like you just saw a ghost." "Nothing." Matt
concentrated on staring out the window. "Did you ever notice how many silver cars there are?" he
said quickly. "That's probably the most popular color, don't you think?" But Tyler wasn't about to
be distracted, especially after Matt had just been teasing him for being afraid. "What's your favorite show?
Who's Don Carlo, and what are they doing to him?" "Don Carlo is the main character in
an opera," Mrs. Whitman explained. "It takes place in the 1500s, during the Spanish Inquisition, but
it's really a tragic love story." Matt stayed silent. It was bad enough that his mother had
jumped into the conversation, but did she have to embarrass him too? "You like opera?" Now it
was Tyler's turn to widen his eyes in horror. "Matt loves opera." Mrs. Whitman corrected him.
"We always listen to the opera program when we're driving around, doing errands on Saturdays. Right, Matt?"
Matt just grunted. His mom was making things worse. They needed to get onto another topic immediately.
His mind whirred with possibilities, but he quickly settled on the local baseball team, the Philadelphia
Phillies. "Did you see that outfielder—" "You do mean opera as in . . ." Tyler cleared
his throat, clasped his hands together, and made a serious face. "Mi-mi-mi-mi-mi," he sang, imitating an opera
star warming up. "Something like that?" He looked at Matt with a huge grin on his face.
"Not exactly." Matt could tell that Tyler was enjoying this way too much. "Or is it
more like this? La-la-la-la-la-la-la-la." Tyler used as deep a voice as possible to sing down the scale.
"No. Not at all." "You should try listening to an opera, Tyler," Mrs. Whitman said as they
arrived in front of Tyler's house. "You might actually enjoy it." "No, thanks, but thanks for
the ride," Tyler said. He pulled his backpack and the pillow and his sleeping bag and the
bulging pillowcase from the car. He struggled up the driveway, but Matt didn't offer to help. Instead
Matt got out of the car and switched to the front seat. "How could you do
that to me, Mom?" he said in a loud, angry voice. "Now everybody knows I like opera!"
"Not everybody, just Tyler," Mrs. Whitman said as she drove away from the curb. "Believe me, it'll
be everybody soon enough. I'm sure Tyler can't wait to tell people." "I'm sorry I embarrassed
you, but liking opera is nothing to be ashamed of. Plenty of people enjoy opera." "Adults like
opera," Matt corrected her. "Kids think it's weird. Weren't you listening to Tyler? Everyone will be making
fun of me as soon as he starts spreading the news. I don't want to go
to school on Monday." "Oh, Matt, that's two days away. I'm sure Tyler will have forgotten all
about it by then." Mrs. Whitman looked over at Matt. "What's that old expression? 'He'd forget his
head if it wasn't attached.' That's Tyler. Now let's enjoy the opera." The orchestra was playing the
overture, which ended in an ominous thunder of drums. "I can already tell from the music
that this is going to be a dark opera." Mrs. Whitman smiled at Matt. "You know you'll
like this once it gets started." "I don't even know who's singing today," Matt grumbled. "And thanks
to you and Tyler, I missed the synopsis of act 1, so I'll have no idea
what's going on until they give the synopsis of act 2." "Well, Don Carlo is the son
of the king of Spain, and his father—" "Never mind," snapped Matt. "I'll figure it out as
we go along." "But it's in Italian!" Matt rolled his eyes. "I don't have to understand
the words to enjoy the music!" He reached over and turned up the volume on the radio.
As soon as Tyler and Brian walked into music class on Monday, they ambushed Matt. "So, I
hear you're a real opera fan." Brian grinned. "Did your car windows shatter while you were listening
on Saturday?" "Ah-ah-ah-ah-ah-ah-ah-ACK!" Tyler sang, sliding up the scale until he ended in a high-pitched squeak.
"I'm glad I left the car before the shrieking—I mean singing —started." Matt put his books under
his chair and sat down. "Nobody broke any glass, you guys. That only happens in cartoons." "Well,
how long did that opera last anyway?" Brian said. "They usually go on for hours and hours,
right?" "Days and nights!" Tyler chimed in. "It didn't last that long." Matt tried to peer around
them to see what the teacher, Mrs. Menendez, had written on the board. "How can you even
understand what's happening when it's all in a foreign language?" Tyler said. Matt sighed heavily. "You
two are awfully curious about opera for people who can't stand it." "Oh, we're just trying to
keep up with your latest activity," Brian said in a mockingly cheerful voice. "We want—" "Time for
class!" Mrs. Menendez clapped her hands. Brian took his seat next to Matt while Tyler sat behind
them. "Before we return to our discussion of Baroque music, I'd like to make a plea for
your help," Mrs. Menendez said. "I desperately need more people to join the school chorus, especially boys."
"No way," Tyler muttered. Mrs. Menendez went on. "I don't know what any of you sound
like because we don't sing in this class. But I'm sure there's some real talent lurking out
there, just waiting to be discovered." Brian elbowed Matt. "Sounds like something you should try, Opera Fan."
"No way! I'm not doing that !" Matt said. Tyler and Brian snickered loudly, and the teacher
looked in their direction. "Is there a problem, boys?" "No, Mrs. Menendez," Matt said. "We thought Matt
was volunteering for chorus," Brian said as Matt glared at him. "Well, you should all consider trying
out." Mrs. Menendez smiled hopefully at the boys. Matt ducked his head and stared at his
hands. He liked to sing, but he wasn't going to give his friends any more ammunition in
their war on opera. He also liked Mrs. Menendez's class. He especially enjoyed it when she played
recordings to illustrate her points about composers. Today she was talking about Handel. "You might know him
from Messiah , his famous choral piece that's often performed at Christmas," Mrs. Menendez said. "But Handel
composed other kinds of music, too, including many operas." At the word "operas," Tyler leaned forward and
tapped Matt on the head with his pencil. "Ow!" Matt rubbed his head. This was going
to be a long class. *** When music finally ended, Matt braced himself for another round of
teasing from his friends. But Tyler was too busy searching through his books and notebooks to say
anything. "I know it's here somewhere," he mumbled as he opened his social studies book and shook
it. "What did you lose?" Matt asked. "My social studies homework. It's not here, so I must
have left it at home." "Well, you're in trouble now," Brian said. "You know homework counts as
part of our grade." "Yeah, thanks, I'm aware of that." "Maybe you could call home and
have someone send it by drone," Matt said as they left the music room. "It'll take us
a few minutes to walk to class." "Great idea!" Brian laughed, but Tyler was not amused. "Hey,
look!" Matt grabbed Brian's arm. "Isn't that Becky walking with Jameson? She keeps looking over here like
she wants to make sure you see she has a new boyfriend." Brian pretended to be very
interested in getting a drink from the water fountain. "What's she doing now?" he whispered. "Whoa! She's
kissing him right here in the hall!" Matt exclaimed. "What?" Brian stood up so quickly that
he lost his grip on his books. They tumbled to the floor. This time it was Tyler's
turn to laugh. "Gotcha!" Matt said as Brian frantically scanned the crowded hallway for his Becky. "You
deserved that for volunteering me for chorus." Matt was glad to be the one doing the teasing
instead of getting grief from his friends. For the rest of the day he laughed every time
Tyler made kissing noises at Brian, or Brian waved his hand like a drone circling for a
landing. After school Matt had to see his science teacher to make up a test. When
he finished, he still had fifteen minutes before the late bus arrived to take him home. It
was raining pretty hard, so he decided to wait inside the school. He was feeling happy because
the science test had been easy. So, as he waited, he hummed a song to himself. Actually
it was more than just a song. It was "Nessun Dorma," an aria from Turandot , a
famous opera. Matt had listened to it so many times that he knew most of the words,
even though they were in Italian. He started out humming softly, but gradually he sang louder
and louder as he realized the empty corridor had great acoustics. Just as he reached the highest
note, the door to the teachers' lounge flew open and Mrs. Menendez rushed out. "Was that you
singing, Matt?" "Uh . . . well . . . um." Matt didn't know what to say,
but then he remembered what his mother always said: you can never go wrong with an apology.
"I'm so sorry. I didn't mean to disturb anyone." "You weren't disturbing me at all. I had
to come out and see who was singing. You have a fabulous soprano voice! You absolutely
have to join chorus!" Matt was flattered, but there was no way he was doing anything musical
after the way his friends had reacted today. "Oh, no, I couldn't possibly do that because I
have—" He stopped while he tried to think up an excuse. Mrs. Menendez jumped right in. "Whatever
you're doing, cancel it! Chorus is the activity for you!" Matt wished she would go back into
the teachers' room, but she kept talking to him and piling on the compliments. "That's amazing that
you can sing 'Nessun Dorma'! Most kids have never heard of it. And your voice—so beautiful!
You have a wonderful gift that you should share with everyone before your voice changes." "I think
my bus is coming!" Matt finally said in desperation. Then he ran outside into the pouring rain.
Matt spent the rest of the week trying to avoid Mrs. Menendez. Normally he looked forward to music
class, but now he was glad he only had it once a week. He didn't want his friends to
hear her praising his voice and pressuring him to join chorus. She really was his favorite teacher, and
he hated saying no to her, and he did like to sing, but . . . He liked
to sing by himself, not with a group of kids, and certainly not where Tyler and Brian could hear
him. All of a sudden, Mrs. Menendez seemed to be everywhere Matt was: in the school library, the
cafeteria, and especially the hallways. But somehow Matt managed to stay out of her way—even when he panicked
on Wednesday and came within an inch of walking into the girls' bathroom by mistake. By the time Friday
came, he was exhausted from dodging her. So he was happy when his mother announced at breakfast on
Saturday that she had a nice surprise for him. "Instead of listening to an opera on the radio today,
how would you like to actually see one?" "Great!" Matt said. "Do you mean the opera in Philadelphia?
Or—" He paused because the other possibility was so exciting, he could barely say the words. "Or are
we going to the Metropolitan Opera in New York City?" "No, we're not going to the Met." Mrs. Whitman
laughed. "That's way too expensive, and besides we couldn't get there in time. We're going to see an
opera at a movie theater." "Oh." Matt made a face as he scooped up another spoonful of cereal.
"Now don't be disappointed." Matt's mom explained that the movie theater was showing a series of operas broadcast live
from famous opera houses. "Today's opera is The Barber of Seville , and it'll be just like seeing
the live production. You might even like it more because you'll have a better view of the stage."
"Oh! That would be great!" Matt said enthusiastically. "Which movie theater are we going to?" "The one near the
mall." "Oh, no! We definitely can't go there. What if we run into someone I know?" "How is
that a problem?" Mrs. Whitman looked puzzled. "If we see friends of yours, that just means they like
opera too. In fact, would you like to invite Tyler to come along? He seemed curious about Don Carlo
last week. I could try to get another ticket online." "No! No! No! That wouldn't be good at
all." Mrs. Whitman crossed her arms and gave an annoyed sigh. "I thought you'd like to do this, but
if you don't want to go—" "You don't understand, Mom. Zombie Invasion 4 is opening this weekend, and
everyone will be going to see it." "Do you really think your friends would go without you? You
won't run into them." Matt had to admit it was highly unlikely that Brian and Tyler would see the
movie without him, but that still didn't solve his problem. "That movie theater has a dozen screens! The
odds we'll run into somebody I know in the lobby or parking lot are huge!" "And if we
do—" "You just don't get it!" Matt slammed his spoon so hard, milk splashed out of his bowl. He
stormed out of the kitchen. Up in his room, he turned on his computer. He'd seen clips of
operas online before, but he'd never watched an entire production. The trouble was that he did want to
see this opera; he just didn't want to see it at that theater. Maybe it was playing somewhere else.
He went online and quickly found The Barber of Seville and where it was showing. Now all he
had to do was persuade his mother to go to one of those other theaters. He came back
downstairs, where she had just finished breakfast. "I know you don't like driving on highways, and there's no other
way to get to that theater," he began. "But what if we went to the movies in Doylestown?
You always say you like the drive up there." "That's almost an hour away!" Mrs. Whitman said. "Besides, I
already bought tickets to this theater." Matt and his mom stood in the kitchen, staring at each other.
He didn't know what else to say, but she did. "Be ready to go at 11 o'clock or
I'm leaving without you. I've heard these shows are crowded, so we need to get there early to find
good seats." Matt went back to his room. There had to be some way that he could go
to the opera without anyone seeing him. But he had no idea how to do that. With a
sigh, he went back online and browsed his favorite websites. He was looking at some photos from famous operas
when he had an idea. "I'll go in disguise!" he thought. "People do that all the time in
operas." He remembered how a character in The Magic Flute , a beautiful young girl, disguised herself as
an old woman. Suddenly he realized how easy it would be to disguise himself as an old man. Matt's
grandfather had lived with them until he died. "I think we still have some of his old clothes
in the spare bedroom," Matt thought. He went off to explore the bureau and closet. He was so
busy digging around that he almost didn't hear his mother. "Matt!" she called from downstairs. "It's after 11 o'clock!
Are you coming or not?" "Coming!" he shouted. A few minutes later, he ran downstairs wearing his grandfather's
hat with a scarf wrapped around the lower part of his face. He was also wearing his own sunglasses
and carrying his grandfather's cane. "A disguise?" Matt's mom just shook her head. "I guess you were serious
about not wanting anyone to see you at the opera." At the theater Mrs. Whitman stopped to buy
some snacks at the counter in the lobby. Matt looked around nervously. "Do you have to do that?" he
asked. "You'll want something to eat later on," she said. "This opera lasts two and a half hours,
and that doesn't include intermission." By the time they walked into the theater where the opera was showing,
it was full. The only seats left were in the front row, but Matt didn't mind one bit! As
the overture started, he removed his sunglasses and settled back in his seat, ready to enjoy the show.
Although Matt was in a movie theater, he felt as if he were watching The Barber
of Seville at an opera house. On the screen the curtains opened to reveal an elaborate
set—a two-story house on a plaza. "Whoa! That looks so real! Where is that?" he whispered
to his mother. "Seville, a city in Spain." It took Matt a few minutes to
get used to watching the action and reading the English subtitles at the same time. But
he soon caught on to the story, even though the performers were singing in Italian. The
wealthy Count Almaviva had fallen in love with Rosina, the daughter of Dr. Bartolo. The count
followed Rosina home and stood under her window, serenading her. "He's a good singer!" Matt whispered.
His mom nodded. Along came Figaro, the barber of Seville, a clever fellow who seemed to
know all the local gossip. Figaro told the count that Dr. Bartolo was not Rosina's father,
but was instead her guardian, who intended to marry her. Meanwhile Rosina looked out her window
and fell instantly in love with the count. "Opera characters are always falling in love
at first sight." Mrs. Whitman shook her head. "I'm not sure that's a good thing." Matt
knew they shouldn't be talking, but he was having fun and so far, no one seemed
to mind. The rich count was now telling Rosina that he was a poor music student.
He wanted to be sure that she loved him and not his money. "I'm not the
only one in disguise today," Matt thought. He felt hot in the crowded theater, so he
looked around to make sure there was no one he knew. Then he took off his
grandfather's hat and scarf. On-screen the two men plotted how the count could get into Rosina's
house to meet her. Figaro suggested the count disguise himself as a soldier who needed
a place to stay; the law required citizens to host soldiers. "Wait!" Matt said loudly. "Now
the count is pretending to be a soldier? This guy has two disguises, and we're only
at the beginning of this thing!" "Shh!" a woman behind him said. "Yes," his mom whispered,
putting her finger to her lips. Matt watched the rest of the first act in silence.
He liked the colorful costumes and the gigantic set, and he recognized some of the music
from TV ads. He especially liked when a donkey danced across the stage. Rosina and the
count's romance grew more complicated as the doctor became suspicious of them. The count abandoned
his military disguise. Matt laughed at the twists and turns of the plot. At intermission Mrs.
Whitman got up to stretch her legs, but Matt remained in his seat, sipping soda and
munching popcorn. The theater lights stayed low because there was still action on-screen. Cameras backstage at
the opera house showed breathless singers hurrying offstage. Stagehands in black shirts and pants moved the
next set into place. After a few more minutes, singers began to step into position for
Act Two. Matt was so fascinated by what was happening behind the scenes that he almost
didn't recognize the woman who walked in front of him. "Mrs. Menendez?" he thought as the
woman dropped into a seat. He wanted to turn to look at her, but he
was afraid she'd notice him. As Act Two began, he slipped on his grandfather's hat and
scarf. This time the count was disguised as a new music teacher who came to Rosina's
house. The count told Rosina's father that the regular teacher was too sick to give her
a lesson. The young couple sang a duet. "Oh, that was lovely!" Matt's mom whispered after
they had finished. Matt liked the music, but he also liked that the piano moved around
the stage. He could see there was someone underneath it, but that only made it funnier.
The real music teacher soon showed up, and the count and Figaro had to persuade him
to pretend he was deathly ill. Matt laughed as characters dressed as gravediggers chased the
music teacher around the stage. He was so involved in the story and the music that
he forgot all about Mrs. Menendez until the count and Rosina were happily married. But then
he suddenly remembered. "Come on! Let's get out of here," he said to his mother as
the singers took their curtain call. "Just a minute. Don't forget Grandpa's cane, and make sure
you pick up your cup and—" "Matt? Mrs. Whitman?" Matt groaned as Mrs. Menendez bustled over
to greet them. "At first I didn't recognize you under that hat," she said to Matt.
"I like your scarf. You look like an opera star! Did you know that one
of the greatest tenors of all time—Luciano Pavarotti—always wore a scarf?" "Yeah, I know who he
was." Matt looked longingly toward the exit. "I love his recording of 'Nessun Dorma.' Nobody can
sing that aria like Pavarotti." Mrs. Menendez sighed. "It's the best version I've ever heard!" Matt
said before he could stop himself. "Well, it sounds like you're a guy who really loves
opera!" Matt's mom gave him an encouraging look. There was nothing embarrassing about admitting he liked
opera to an adult, but he still swallowed hard before he replied. "I do. We listen
to the opera on the radio every Saturday." "I thought Matt would have fun actually seeing
an opera," Mrs. Whitman said. "What did you think?" Mrs. Menendez asked Matt. "It's so
much better than just listening to the opera. The sets and the costumes and the acting
. . . Everything was amazing!" "And you can see how much effort singing takes at
that level," Mrs. Menendez said. She went on about the opera, and Matt was actually enjoying
himself. He was just about to ask a question when the conversation suddenly turned dangerous. "You
know, Mrs. Whitman, Matt has such a wonderful voice. I've been trying to get him to
join chorus." "Really?" Matt's mom stared at him in surprise. "You never told me that, Matt."
He felt like he was in a horror movie, watching himself get eaten up by a
monster. "I overheard him singing 'Nessun Dorma,' and I couldn't believe his voice. You're his
mother. Perhaps you can persuade him to sing with us." "Don't worry, Mrs. Menendez. He'll be
at chorus from now on. Right, Matt?" Matt stayed silent. "Ugh," he thought with dread. "Wait
till Tyler and Brian hear about this. They're going to give me such a hard time."
Twice a week Matt and his friends spent the last period of the day goofing around in study
hall while pretending to do homework. But now Matt had chorus—a change he dreaded mentioning to Brian
and Tyler. On Matt's first day of rehearsal, the three boys were walking toward study hall as usual,
when Matt stopped outside Mrs. Menendez's room. "I'm in chorus now, so I can't go to study hall
anymore." He quickly pivoted toward the door. "Bye." "Wait! What do you mean you're in chorus now?" Brian
asked. "Are you saying that for real?" Tyler asked. Matt nodded. "When my mom found out that
Mrs. Menendez was looking for guys to join chorus, she made me sign up." Okay, that wasn't exactly
the whole truth. But there was no way he was confessing that he'd run into Mrs. Menendez while
watching an opera with his mother. Or that Mrs. Menendez had caught him belting out an aria.
Or that ever since The Barber of Seville , he'd been thinking he might like to try chorus
after all. "I mean if it was just my mom, I could probably talk her out of it.
Or if it was just Mrs. Menendez, but both of them together . . ." Matt nervously shifted
his books to his left arm. "I didn't stand a chance." "Sounds like that time my dad
and the band teacher made me take trombone lessons in fourth grade," said Brian. "I couldn't argue my
way out of that for anything. What you have to do in this situation is fail, and then
they'll let you quit." Tyler agreed. "Start forgetting to bring your music all the time, and you'll
be back hanging around with us in no time." "Thanks, guys." Matt felt relieved. He had no intention
of failing at chorus, but now he could enjoy singing without worrying about his friends making fun of
him. The bell rang for the start of class, and Matt ducked inside Mrs. Menendez's room. There was
only one empty chair near the back, so Matt took that seat. The girl to his left
immediately started talking to him. "Hi! You must be new! I'm Dede! I mean, my real name's Elizabeth,
but everybody calls me Dede. I'm not sure why—because it's not the usual nickname for Elizabeth—but everybody does."
Dede paused to take a breath, and Matt stared at the girl in the Phillies T-shirt who'd
just given him such an enthusiastic welcome. "Dede." He repeated slowly. "Oh, like Mimi!" Dede looked confused. "You
have an unexpected nickname like Mimi in the opera La Bohème . Her real name is Lucia." Matt
instantly regretted that he'd mentioned an opera. Now Dede probably thought he was showing off. But Dede's face
lit up with recognition. "Oh, Mimi in the opera! Now I get it. I thought you were
talking about somebody named Mimi here at school, and I couldn't think who that would be. I love
that opera, don't you? My dad says there's going to be a production of La Bohème in Philadelphia,
and I'm hoping we can go. It's so sad when Mimi dies at the end, don't you
think? And what's your name?" Matt grinned and told her his name. He wanted to ask if she
had a favorite Phillies player, but Mrs. Menendez was starting to lead the chorus in warm-up exercises. *
* * The weeks passed. Matt began to look forward to rehearsals with Dede, who always had lots
to say about the Phillies and their most recent game. The other kids in chorus were nice
too, and some of the guys even wore hats. Most teachers made kids leave their hats in their
lockers, but Mrs. Menendez liked to encourage her students' individuality. Matt took to smuggling his grandfather's hat into
class, careful that Brian and Tyler never saw it. In fact, it had been a long time
since either friend had mentioned chorus. So Matt was caught off guard one day at lunch. "Haven't you
failed chorus yet? How can you stand those chorus kids?" Brian asked. "They're the worst." Matt blurted out,
hoping that would end the conversation. "What do you mean?" "Oh, you know . . ." Matt was
trying to be vague because he had no idea what he meant. He liked chorus because he
liked singing, and he liked Dede and the other kids. But he could never tell Brian and Tyler
that. He was still trying to think of what to say when Brian suddenly leaped up and ran
across the cafeteria. "What's with him?" Matt asked. Tyler turned around to look at Brian, who was
now talking to Becky. "Jameson broke up with Becky, so Brian's trying to win her back." Matt shook
his head. "It's like . . ." He started to say something but stopped. "Like what?" It was
like the on-again, off-again romance of some of the characters in La Bohème ! Matt was thinking. But
Matt knew better than to say that to Tyler. "Nothing," Matt said quickly. "Did you watch the
Phillies game last night?" That afternoon Mrs. Menendez had an exciting announcement at rehearsal. An opera company in
Philadelphia needed sopranos to play street urchins in La Bohème . "I encourage you all to try out—boys
as well as girls—and I'll be happy to help you with audition music." Some kids announced they
didn't like opera, and some said they couldn't attend all the rehearsals in Philadelphia. But Matt and Dede
high-fived and said together, "We're doing this!" For two weeks Mrs. Menendez worked with them every day after
school. As they learned the music, she helped them improve their pronunciation of the Italian lyrics. On the
afternoon of the audition, she even drove them to Philadelphia. Matt and Dede were both nervous, but
their teacher reassured them that they were prepared—and they were. After the audition she took them to a
café near the theater. "We'll go here every day after rehearsals," said Dede, dipping a French fry in
ketchup. "Oh! We have to plan how we'll get to rehearsals because we'll have to leave school
early. My dad can drive us sometimes, but can your mom take us some days? This is going
to be so much fun!" "Assuming we get parts," Matt said cautiously. "We'll get parts." Dede smiled and
popped another French fry into her mouth. A few days later, Matt received an email from the opera
company. He immediately texted Dede. "I got a part! Did you?" "NO!" She texted back, sending a
sad face too. "What?" Matt stared at his phone in disappointment. This wasn't in their plans at all.

"Who am I supposed to hang out with?" Matt grumbled. It was the first day of rehearsals for La Bohème , and Matt wasn't happy. Without Dede as a fellow street urchin, he had to go to Philadelphia all by himself. Inside the theater he walked through a maze of corridors. He
came to a dead end near the costume shop. "Where is this rehearsal room anyway?" If Dede were there, they'd be laughing about getting lost, but now Matt felt anxious. He retraced his steps
and finally found the right door. Matt took a deep breath to calm himself and walked into a room filled with kids,
all talking at once. Mr. Lorenzo, the chorus master, gave a shrill whistle. "Okay, people, let's get started! Settle down and introduce yourselves." One by one, the kids stood up and said their own
names as well as the names of any operas they'd appeared in. One girl had been in six operas! Matt sighed loudly, and the boy next to him leaned over. "Not everyone has
that much experience," he reassured Matt. "If you're here, you're a good singer. I'm Tim, by the way." "Thanks, Tim," Matt

magic acts." The boys quieted down but most weren't looking at Mr. Carlson. Frank was staring
at his phone, clearly bored now that he'd described the show he'd seen. Amy put up
her hand. "You don't have to raise your hand during club meetings," Mr. Carlson said. "Okay."
Amy hesitated. The teacher's comment had thrown her off track. "Well, first there are illusions. Those
are the big tricks you usually see onstage. Things like levitating a person or sawing a
woman in half." She glared at Frank, but he was still looking at his phone. "You
know, things with fireworks or explosives." Frank was paying attention now. "Right," said Mr. Carlson. "Illusions
often use special equipment to achieve their effects. When the magician is onstage, he—and I use
the word he because most magicians are men—doesn't really have to do much. He's more of
a performer than someone who's mastered a set of skills. What else?" "Escapes!" said Frank. "Tricks
that make the audience worry the magician might die." "Yeah!" a couple boys said. "Escape tricks
don't have to be dangerous," said Mr. Carlson. "Some of the most interesting and intricate escapes
involve ropes and knots. Keep going." "Does mind reading count?" Brett asked. "It sure does," Mr.
Carlson said. "Sometimes the magician is blindfolded or turns his back to the audience. Then
he has to guess what kind of object an audience member is holding up." Amy's hand
shot up. "But there's no such thing as mind reading, right? I mean, nobody can really
do that." "You're correct." Mr. Carlson nodded at Amy. "Those tricks usually involve signals between the
magician and his assistant. But we still haven't mentioned several kinds of magic." "Making things appear
and disappear!" Amy said. "Right. They can be small things—like cards or coins—that you hold in
your hand. Or big things like a person. One magician even made the Statue of Liberty
disappear on TV! All right, who can define sleight of hand for me?" Amy raised her
hand again. Frank sighed. "You don't have to raise your hand, Ms. Encyclopedia of Magic. And
you don't have to answer every question." Amy could feel her anger rising, but then she
remembered Megan's advice to ignore him. " Sleight of hand can actually be two different things,"
she said calmly. "Some people use the phrase to refer to those small tricks you mentioned.
The ones with coins or cards or anything you can hide in your hand. But other
people use it to describe any deceptive move a magician makes with her hands. The magician
does that to misdirect the audience's attention." Mr. Carlson smiled at Amy. "Excellent! Okay, everyone, let's
see what you can do." The teacher laid an assortment of props—cards, rings, scarves, and coins—on
a table. "Who wants to go first?" Frank strode confidently to the table and picked up
the rings. He did a fast-paced routine, linking and unlinking them in the blink of an
eye. When he finished, Amy joined in the applause. Frank was a pain, but she had
to admit he was a good magician. Next Brett picked up the cards and pulled out
three. He held them out toward Amy. "Pick a card." She picked the one on the
left. "No, not that one!" She picked the one on the right. He groaned "Not that
one either!" "Okay, time for our first lesson." Mr. Carlson grinned. "I assume you wanted her
to pick the one in the middle?" Brett nodded. "So you have to do what magicians
call the force . When she picks the first card, you say, 'Great! You've eliminated one.'
Then when she picks the second card, you throw that one down, and say, 'Smart choice.'
And then you use the third card to do your trick. Now, does anyone know why
it's called the force ?" Amy knew. "Because you're forcing the person to choose the card
you need for your trick." "And what was that trick anyway?" Frank rolled his eyes. "Uh
. . ." Brett stepped away from the table. "You know, I don't really remember how
that one goes." Amy felt bad for Brett. She also felt more and more nervous the
closer it came to her turn. To calm herself, she picked up a card and practiced
concealing it in her palm. By now seven kids had performed and only four were left.
Mr. Carlson glanced at the clock. "I'm afraid our time is up. The rest of you
can show us your tricks next week." "Whew!" Amy let out a loud sigh of relief.
As Amy was leaving the first meeting of the magic club, Mr. Carlson stopped her.
"I noticed that you seemed nervous about performing," the teacher said kindly. "You know, some
people are really good at mastering the mechanics of a trick, while others are better at
performing. It's the rare kid who's a skilled magician and a spellbinding performer." Amy nervously
shifted her backpack from one shoulder to the other. "Ugh," she thought. "Here comes another
lecture on being more outgoing." Everyone—from her parents to her teachers to Megan—was always telling
her that she needed to be bolder and speak up more. "I watched how you were
palming that card," Mr. Carlson said. "That takes a lot of skill. How did you
learn to do that?" Amy was puzzled by such an obvious question. "Practice, of course."
"That's exactly how you learn to be a better performer," Mr. Carlson went on. "I
also saw that some of the boys weren't exactly welcoming you. What if you could use
your fear of performing to your advantage? I think you could impress the boys at
the same time. Are you familiar with the trick where you pass a coin through
a table?" "Oh, yeah!" Amy's eyes lit up with excitement. "I did that at a
restaurant once to keep my little cousin amused while we were waiting for dinner." "If
you can do that trick well, the boys might start giving you more respect. It's often
done at a dining table. But you could use my desk." Amy looked at the
jumble of papers, books, and office supplies covering her teacher's desk. She laughed. "I guess
you'll have to clean it off first!" *** The idea behind the coin trick was
simple, but it required split-second timing. At the restaurant a saltshaker had played a key role;
for school Amy decided to substitute Mr. Carlson's coffee cup. Over the next week, she
practiced every spare moment. Mr. Carlson helped her to develop some patter. That was the
magicians' word for the story that accompanies a trick. At the next magic club meeting,
Amy was nervous about the idea of outwitting the boys. But she also felt excited. If
the trick went well, it would be fun to see their faces. She sat behind
Mr. Carlson's desk, which he had cleaned off. On the surface she placed a nickel
and his coffee cup. First, she rapped on his desk to show that it was
solid. "Every day Mr. Carlson sits at this desk, correcting math homework. Little does he
realize that it's more than a desk. It's actually a portal, a gateway that objects can
pass through." Amy looked at the boys, who were now staring at the gray metal
desk. "All he needs is this magic poncho!" With a flourish, she laid a paper
napkin on the desk. Everyone laughed, but this time the boys weren't laughing at her.
They were laughing at the "magic poncho" prop. "I will now use this cup and this
magic poncho to make this coin pass through the desk." Amy covered the coin with
the cup and then placed the napkin over the cup. She closed her eyes, waved
her hands in circles, and tapped the cup. Her eyes flew open. She took a
breath and reached for the cup. The nickel was still there. "I knew she couldn't do
it." Frank smirked and looked at the other boys. "Oh no! That didn't work!" Amy
appeared flustered. But as she glanced at Mr. Carlson, he winked at her. They both
knew this was part of the act. "Oh, please, Mr. Carlson. Let me try that
again. I know I can do it right." "Well, I don't know . . ." Mr.
Carlson hesitated. The boys looked back and forth between the teacher and Amy, who seemed
on the verge of tears. "All right. One more time, but that's it." Amy placed
the coin under the cup and the cup under the napkin. She closed her eyes,
waved her hands in circles, and tapped the cup. As her eyes popped open, she
slammed her hand on the napkin-covered cup. She lifted the napkin. The coin was still there,
but the cup was gone. "Ahh!" the boys gasped. "Sorry, Mr. Carlson." Amy pulled his
coffee cup from under the desk. "I guess that portal only works for cups!" The
boys broke into applause. Even Frank admitted it was a pretty good trick. "Do it
again," he demanded. "Oh, no," Mr. Carlson said. "Never repeat a trick. Surprise is one of
the elements that make a trick work. If you repeat it, people will be watching
to see how it's done." "Besides"—Amy grinned—"a magician never reveals her secrets." *** Every week
Mr. Carlson taught the kids a new trick and had them perform the previous week's
trick. Frank usually performed best when they first learned a trick. But Amy was the one
who always mastered the trick. That was because, unlike Frank, she went home and practiced
until she could do the trick effortlessly. Meanwhile poor Brett struggled, and Amy tried to
help him. As the weeks passed, Amy began to look forward to magic club. She
got better at making up patter for the tricks. But she still wasn't comfortable talking
to any of the boys except Brett. Until someone arrived unexpectedly one afternoon. The club was
in the middle of a meeting when Megan burst through the door. "I just quit
the musical!" she announced breathlessly. "Ms. Patel—she's the director—didn't think I was serious enough! Can
you believe that? She said I was always talking. And she was mad that I
missed two rehearsals in a row!" All the boys were staring wide-eyed at Megan. Mr. Carlson
started to speak. "Well—" "Ms. Patel gave my part to somebody else and put me
in the chorus. It's so unfair! I've had more years of voice and dance lessons
than everybody else combined! So I quit. And now I can join magic club!" Megan
flopped into a seat. "Well, the more the merrier," Mr. Carlson said. "Welcome!" Frank rolled his
eyes and muttered, "Another girl magician." Amy broke into a grin. Now there was another
girl in the club, and she wasn't just any girl. She was Amy's best friend.
At first Amy thought it would be fun to have Megan in magic club, but she
quickly began to change her mind. As soon as Megan showed up, she was a distraction.
Mr. Carlson had been in the middle of demonstrating a rope trick, but he had to
stop to introduce Megan. Then Megan couldn't just sit quietly; she had to say something special
to each boy. "As I was saying . . ." Mr. Carlson picked up the rope
again. "This is a classic example of something appearing other than it is. This looks like
a rope with a knot in it, but—" "Brett keeps glancing over here," Megan whispered to
Amy. "Uh-huh." Amy was trying to pay attention to the teacher. Megan nudged Amy in the
side. "I think he's looking at you ! Maybe he likes—" "Please be quiet, Megan! I
can't concentrate on this trick!" Amy burst out. Suddenly everyone—not just Brett—was looking at the two
girls. "Um . . ." Amy felt her face growing hot with embarrassment. "Girls!" Frank grinned
and pretended to scold them. "Some of us are actually trying to learn something here." Megan
frowned at Frank. "Mr. Carlson, when do we learn how to make people disappear?" "That's an
advanced lesson, and you have to learn how to make them reappear." "Maybe not," Megan said
in a low voice that the teacher couldn't hear. But everyone around her heard, and all
the boys laughed. Frank just glared at her. * * * As the weeks passed, Amy
continued to have mixed feelings about Megan's joining the club. On the one hand, it was
nice to have another girl around. But it was clear to Amy that Megan was only
there to meet boys. She had no real interest in magic. "Do we have to go
to magic club this afternoon?" Megan asked Amy as they opened their lockers at the end
of school one day. "Of course!" Amy was looking forward to going. Megan threw her books
in her locker and took out her coat. "That stuff Mr. Carlson shows us is too
difficult. He says you always have to be two steps ahead of the audience, but I
feel like I'm two steps behind. I don't want to learn those tricks. I just want
to be onstage." Amy felt annoyed. "Look, Megan, you don't have to come if you don't
want to. But I don't want to miss this meeting. Mr. Carlson said we're having a
special guest." "It's probably a rabbit." Megan closed her locker and followed Amy, who was already
walking down the hall. Amy turned around. "No, it won't be a rabbit. Mr. Carlson banned
live animals from our acts on the first day." When they arrived at magic club, an
older woman was talking to the teacher. She had short gray hair and a big smile.
Once everyone arrived, Mr. Carlson introduced his guest. "Kids, I'd like you to welcome Olga Lapinski,
assistant to the late, great Marvin Marvelo, who traveled the world, astounding people with his feats
of magic. Besides being Marvin's wife and assistant, she helped to develop some of his most
famous tricks. Since his tragic death, Olga is the only one who knows the secrets of
his tricks." Olga smiled. "Thank you for inviting me to your meeting." All the kids
applauded except for Frank. He shook his head and muttered, "She's just an assistant. What a
waste of time!" But Megan tapped Amy's arm excitedly. "An assistant! That's what I should do.
I'd be a great assistant!" Olga began speaking. "An assistant is an important part of any
magic act. He or she helps with the trick directly, or helps by distracting the audience.
You should always treat your assistants nicely and pay them well. It's the right thing to
do—and you want to be sure they never betray you!" "Betray you?" said Brett. "What are
you talking about?" "Well, magicians are just like anybody else. Whenever they see a new act,
the first thing they ask is: How did the magician do that? Magicians are always trying
to learn the secrets behind others' tricks, especially the big illusions. One way to do that
is to bribe an assistant to reveal the information." "That's pretty sneaky," Brett said. "Can you
tell us more about what assistants do?" Amy asked. "They get sawed in half." Frank was
now tapping away on his phone. "That's true and sometimes they vanish. When the assistant walks
in front of the magician, she may be acting as a screen between him and the
audience. Or she may be passing him something he needs. Or," Olga said with a wink,
"that may be what the magician wants you to think. Whenever assistants are onstage, they're there
for a reason." "Did you have a favorite costume?" Megan asked. "Well, I always loved sequin-covered
leotards," Olga said. "But—" "Me too!" Megan interrupted. "But my favorite costumes were the ones that
were part of the act. I loved it when I dressed like Marvin. It seemed to
the audience that he was one place onstage when he was really somewhere else." "Now I
have another surprise for you," Mr. Carlson said. "The school is having a carnival in a
few weeks to raise funds for after-school activities. All the teams and clubs will get a
portion of the money. With the help of Olga, I've come up with a grand illusion
that we can perform in the auditorium." "What is it?" a few kids yelled at once.
"In a minute. It will take everyone's help to build the illusion and to work behind
the scenes on carnival night. But we need only one magician and one assistant onstage." Mr.
Carlson paused. "After careful consideration, I've selected Amy as the magician." "Go, Amy!" Megan cried. Frank
crossed his arms and scowled. "That's ridiculous! I'm the best magician in the room." "Please stand
up, Amy," Mr. Carlson said. "I chose you because I know you'll put in the practice
time and your patter has really come a long way." "Thanks," Amy mumbled. She looked down,
struggling to decide if this was a good thing. Then Mr. Carlson made another announcement. "And
now Amy will choose her assistant." Megan popped up and stood next to Amy. She flashed
her brightest smile. "Uh . . . uh . . . actually . . ." Amy
hesitated. Then she said in a strong voice, "I pick Brett." Olga clapped her hands with
delight. "A female magician with a male assistant—I love it!" But not everyone was so happy.
Megan sank back into her seat with a shocked look on her face. Meanwhile Brett came
forward and stood next to Amy. "This is a joke, right?" Megan said. "You meant to choose
me as your assistant." "Sorry, Megan, but I need someone I can rely on, and you
can be, well, kind of undependable sometimes." Amy felt awful. She knew the words were true,
but she didn't want to hurt her friend's feelings. "Well, then, I'm through with this stupid club!"
Megan started to storm out of the room. When she reached the door, she turned back
to Amy. "You wouldn't even be in magic club if it weren't for me!" "I'm done
too." Frank gathered up his backpack. "I don't have time for this bunch of losers. Hey, Megan,
wait up!" "Oh my!" Olga lifted her eyebrows. "I've seen temperamental behavior like that in the
world of professional magic. But I thought kids would be more easygoing." Brett let out his
breath. "Megan and Frank—now, there's a pair who deserve each other." Amy shook her head sadly.
At that moment she had to agree. "All right," Mr. Carlson said. "Before I describe the illusion
for the carnival, does anyone else want to abandon us?" No one made a move to
leave. "Good. Now here's what's going to happen. Amy, assisted by Brett, will make six people
disappear." "Wow!" everyone said at once. "Obviously you kids can't be the people," Olga added, "because everyone
would be suspicious of that." "I'm leaning toward choosing players on the boys' and girls' soccer
teams," Mr. Carlson said. "They're popular kids. Wouldn't a lot of people show up to see
them disappear?" "Yes," Amy said. "But we can't trust other kids to keep the secret behind the
trick. They're not magicians like we are." A few boys nodded. "What about six teachers?" Brett
said. "There are lots of them I'd like to see disappear!" All the kids laughed and
even Mr. Carlson did too. "That's a great idea," Amy said, and everyone else agreed. "Well, that's
settled," Mr. Carlson said. "Now all you have to do, Amy, is find us some teachers
who have the time to participate and can keep a secret." "Oh." Amy felt her heart
sinking. She dreaded talking to teachers, never mind asking them for a favor. "Don't worry!" Brett said
cheerfully. "I'll help you." *** With Brett at her side, Amy visited all the teachers she
knew. Many of them were too busy to attend rehearsals for the magic trick. But slowly
over the next couple weeks, Amy and Brett found six willing teachers. They got them to
sign the secrecy agreement that Mr. Carlson had drafted. Meanwhile, under the supervision of Olga Lapinski and
Mr. Carlson, the other magicians built the frame for a large box. Instead of solid sides,
it had four black curtains, which matched the curtain hanging across the back of the stage.
"How will the teachers escape?" Amy asked. Olga whispered her response, and then said aloud, "That's why
you need the teachers to rehearse, along with friends behind the big black curtain to assist
them." When everyone arrived in the auditorium for the first rehearsal, the box was standing on
a low platform. "Are you ready, Amy?" Mr. Carlson asked. "You're the magician, so you're in charge."
Amy nodded. "Okay, all kids should be offstage. Those of you who'll be wandering the carnival
dressed as magicians can sit in the audience. The rest of you should be backstage." The
kids scrambled into position. Mr. Carlson opened the red curtain at the front of the stage. "Teachers
should be seated separately around the auditorium," Amy called out. But the teachers were too busy
talking to pay attention to her. "Mr. Carlson, they're not listening to me." "You're the magician,"
he repeated. "Attention, teachers!" Amy said in her loudest voice, but they kept on talking. "Here, let
me help." Brett stuck two fingers in his mouth and let out an ear-piercing whistle. The
auditorium went silent, and Amy grinned at Brett. She repeated her instructions to the teachers, who
slowly took their seats. "And they complain when we don't respond right away!" she said to
Brett. "You're doing great! Just show them who's boss." "Okay, let's practice getting onstage and into the
box," she said. "Everybody walk around to the back and step in." "Wait a minute!" Mr.
Harrington called out. He was Amy's social studies teacher. "Why can't we be onstage at the
beginning? Wouldn't it be better if everyone could get a good look at us before we disappear?
Maybe each of us could say something as we enter the box." Amy sighed and looked
at Brett. "You're the boss," he whispered. "I want you in the audience, so it looks
like I've picked random volunteers." "But you haven't picked us at random," Mr. Harrington insisted. "True, but
that's what I want it to look like." "Always be suspicious of the volunteers, my dear
Mr. Harrington." Olga came out from the wings and pointed toward the box. "Won't you come
this way?" She herded him and the rest of the teachers into the box. "Okay, teachers, close
the curtains," said Amy. The curtains on the back and one side closed; the curtain rods
on the front and the other side fell off, taking the curtains with them. Amy sighed
again and called out, "Magic crew! Curtain repair!" That was pretty much how rehearsals went. The teachers
showed up on time, but that was about all they did right. They talked among themselves
and didn't listen to instructions. Mr. Harrington was full of ideas to improve the act, but
none of his ideas were really useful. Amy finally thought of a special role he could
play at the start of the act, and that seemed to satisfy his need to stand out.
Olga worked with Amy on her patter, reminding her to fill the auditorium with her voice
and her presence. "You don't have to do much magic, but you do have to perform,"
Olga said. Amy felt smaller and smaller as every day passed. She wished she had a best
friend to talk to, but Megan had stopped speaking to her weeks ago. After five rehearsals
the only person performing well was Brett. He moved silently across the stage, escorting the teachers
into the box. He whisked open the curtains when it was time to reveal that they had
disappeared. He was perfect, which was a good thing because the carnival was the next night.

episodes.title: Now You See It, Now You Don't

subtitle.text: On carnival night a steady line of people streamed into the school and bought tickets.
By seven o'clock Amy and Brett were walking around the carnival, looking at what the other
clubs and teams were presenting. The magic club's act wasn't scheduled until eight o'clock. Mr.
Carlson figured a good crowd would have arrived by then. Amy and Brett went outside,
where the boys' soccer team was operating a dunk tank. Their coach was sitting on
a small seat above a tank filled with water. "That looks like fun," Brett said. "You
want to try?" "No, you go ahead." Amy was too nervous to do anything but
watch. Brett hurled a ball toward a round target on the tank. If he hit
the target, the seat would flip down and dump the coach into the water. But Brett
missed. "It's probably a good thing I didn't dunk him. He's my gym teacher." Brett
smiled at Amy, but she didn't respond. "Come on, lighten up! You're going to be
great!" Amy groaned. "I don't want to talk about it. Let's go inside." But inside the
school, posters for their magic act hung everywhere. Magic club members were walking around, dressed
in capes and top hats, encouraging people to attend the show. "I wonder if Frank
and Megan will come," Brett said. "I hope Megan comes." Amy scanned the hallway for
her friend. "I can do without Frank." Amy and Brett went into the gym, where the
girls' basketball team was sponsoring a contest to see who could score the most baskets
in one minute. While Brett lined up to take a turn, Amy sat glumly in
the bleachers. "Hey, Amy!" Amy turned. "Megan!" "I just wanted to wish you luck. I—" "Oh,
Megan, I've missed you!" Amy hugged her friend. "I'm so nervous! Please tell me you'll
come to the show." "Of course I'll come! Are you sure you want me there?
I've been acting like such a jerk." Amy patted the spot next to her. "Sit while
I wait for Brett." Megan sat down, and the two friends watched the action on
the court. When it was Brett's turn to shoot, he searched the bleachers for Amy.
He finally spotted her and gave her a thumbs-up. "Well, that's interesting," Megan said. "I'm
sure he likes you." "I can't think about that now." The two girls watched as Brett
missed every basket. "I want to sample some of the cooking club's food." Megan stood
up as Brett came over. "But I'll be at your show." Amy and Brett made
their way to the auditorium, where they went backstage and checked that everything was ready. Amy
put on her top hat and picked up her magic wand. At ten minutes before
show time, she peeked into the audience. "I see all the teachers except Mr. Harrington."
Brett sighed in exasperation. "I'll find him. And if I can't, we'll go on without
him." Five minutes later Brett returned. "He was in the teachers' lounge. By the way, I
saw Frank lurking in the back of the auditorium. The place is packed!" Amy nervously
tapped her wand against her leg. "Great! More people to watch me fail." "You want
to go over your patter one more time?" Brett asked. "No, that'll only make things worse."
Mr. Carlson came backstage. He checked in with the kids who were positioned behind the
black curtain at the rear of the stage, and then he came over to Amy
and Brett. "You two ready?" Amy hid her shaking hands behind her back so he couldn't
see them. "I guess so." "She's ready, Mr. Carlson. She'll be great!" Brett said. "Then
it's showtime!" Mr. Carlson stepped before the red stage curtain at the front of the
stage. "Good evening! Tonight the magic club has a special treat for you. The Amazing
Amy will make someone disappear right before your eyes! Or as we magicians say, 'Now you
see it, now you don't.'" As the crowd politely clapped, Amy and Brett stepped in
front of the red curtain. The lights were bright, but Amy could see Megan smiling
in the front row. She took a deep breath and began. "A magician usually makes his
lovely female assistant vanish. But as you can see, I don't have a female assistant."
She held out her hand and Brett bowed. "He's still lovely!" someone called out from
the audience. Mr. Carlson had told Amy to anticipate that response, so she was ready.
"He sure is!" she replied, and Brett took another bow. "But I think it'd be more
interesting to make a whole group of people disappear, don't you?" "Yes!" the crowd roared.
The red curtain opened to reveal the box with its black curtains open. "The only
question is: Which group?" "Cheerleaders!" someone called out. "Baseball players!" "Teachers!" Amy smiled slowly as if
that were the first time she'd considered this idea. "Ah, yes, teachers!" Amy turned to
Brett. "Please find six brave volunteers." Brett went into the audience and returned with the
teachers. He escorted them to the box and helped them step inside. "Wait! There are only
five teachers!" Amy pretended to sigh with annoyance as she looked into the audience. "I
need one more volunteer." She shielded her eyes from the light with her hand. "Aha!
There's one!" Mr. Harrington left his seat and hurried onstage. So far the act was
going according to plan. "If I disappear forever, my classes still have a test on Monday!"
Mr. Harrington shouted. Amy was annoyed by his ad-lib. "Should I make him disappear forever?"
she asked the crowd. "Yes!" they roared. "You wouldn't do that to your favorite teacher,"
he said. "Into the box!" Amy pointed her wand at Mr. Harrington, and the audience laughed
at their banter. "Teachers! Close the curtains!" Amy commanded. Brett walked around the box to
show that there was no way the teachers could secretly slip behind the stage curtains.
"Making people disappear is a time-honored tradition in the magic world," Amy said. "But where do
they go when they vanish? Do they momentarily step into another dimension? Who knows? None
of them ever recall where they've been." She waved her wand. "Abracadabra! Make these teachers
disappear!" She faced the audience as Brett dramatically pulled all the box's curtains open. "Ohh!"
the audience cried. Amy smiled and turned toward the box. The teachers had disappeared. With the
exception of Mr. Harrington. Amy looked at Brett in horror. That wasn't supposed to happen!
For a moment Amy stood frozen in the spotlight. Why hadn't Mr. Harrington disappeared? Her heart
sank. What was she going to do now? Finally she just shrugged. "Why is there always
a teacher around when you don't want one?" The audience burst into loud laughter, and Mr.
Carlson returned to the stage. "Let's give a big hand for the Amazing Amy!" he said
to the crowd. "Nice recovery," he said to her. Brett reached up and helped Mr. Harrington down
from the box. They joined Amy at the front of the stage, where the three of
them bowed. "It was so dark in there!" a flustered Mr. Harrington whispered to Amy. "I
don't know what went wrong, but I didn't have time to escape." "Don't worry about it.
Just keep smiling." Amy waved as they left the stage. But the audience was demanding a
curtain call, so Amy, Brett, and Mr. Harrington held hands and came out for another bow.
This time the five teachers who had disappeared ran into the auditorium from the main doors.
"Boo! The teachers are back!" someone yelled. Amy grinned. "Yep. I didn't really make them disappear
forever!" The teachers joined her and the others onstage. Everyone in the audience leaped to their feet
and began clapping wildly. Brett squeezed Amy’s hand. "I told you that you’d be great!" She
smiled and took another bow. After the show Megan rushed to congratulate Amy outside the auditorium.
"That was unbelievable! I saw the teachers go into the box, but I didn't see them
get out. I'm thinking they must have exited from the back of the box, but how?"
Amy smiled mysteriously. "It was magic!" "So you can't even tell your best friend?" "Nope." Amy
laughed. "That was sensational!" a parent said as he passed by in the crowded hallway. "Thanks!"
Amy replied. A little girl ran up to Amy with a scrap of paper and a
pen. "Can I have your autograph? I want to be a girl magician too!" Amy smiled and
signed her name. "Everybody is talking about you!" Megan held up her phone so Amy could
see the screen. "You should ask Mr. Carlson if you can do another magic act for
the whole school. That would make a great assembly!" Amy shook her head. "I proved to
everyone that I could pull off a big illusion and entertain an auditorium full of people.
But I didn't really enjoy it. I don't like depending on an assistant or a group
of volunteers. And I don't like waiting for somebody to build an illusion for me. I
like—" "Oh, I get it." Megan cut her off. "You want to be a star all
by yourself." "That's not it at all." Amy put down the duffel bag containing her hat

to give Parker bad advice—even as a joke. "But I'd never hurt him!" he said
to himself. By the time Lakshmi and Ben returned with some ice, Parker was sitting up.
After applying ice for a few minutes, he was able to stand with Mr. Stein's
help. Everyone in the auditorium applauded. "Way to go, Parker!" Ray slapped him on the
back as he limped past. "Leave me alone!" Parker snapped. Ray stayed silent, watching as
his friend exited stage left. *** Parker took a few days off from rehearsing to
rest his knee. He still came to rehearsals, but he sat in the auditorium while
Ray played Warbucks. Whenever Ray tried to talk to him, Parker started talking to someone else.
One day Ray looked out from the stage and saw Parker surrounded by girls. They
included Lakshmi, Kyla, and all of Kyla's friends. Ray came offstage in time to hear
Parker explaining that he had to pay attention. "Just in case Ms. Kwan changes one
of the plays onstage." "This isn't soccer," Ray muttered as he passed. "It's called blocking
. That's the right word for how actors move around the stage." "Did he just
call you a blockhead?" Kyla asked. "Who knows?" Parker smiled and shrugged. "Now, who brought me
some cookies today? Those chocolate ones from yesterday were delicious!" Ray rolled his eyes. While
he had lost most of his friends, Parker was making new ones by the minute.
After the break Ray had to rehearse a scene as Officer Ward. He stood in
the wings, waiting for his cue. He watched as Annie sang "Tomorrow" with Sandy. He
wished he could talk to Lakshmi. But what would he say? That his "jokes" had gone
too far? That maybe, if he really thought about it, he had been trying to
steal Parker's role? But he would never do anything to hurt Parker? Yes, that was
perfect. When the orphan and dog stopped singing, Officer Ward entered and confronted them. "Stop
right there!" Ms. Kwan frowned at Ray. "Why are you smiling, Officer Ward? This dog
doesn't have a leash or a license. You're trying to enforce the law here." "Sorry.
I was thinking of something else." "Make your entrance again." Ray went back offstage. This time
he entered as a stern policeman. He looked mean as he threatened to send Sandy
to the dog pound. "Much better, Ray," Ms. Kwan said when they finished the scene.
"That's it for today, everybody." She went over to talk to Parker. Ray waited while
Mr. Stein gave Annie and Sandy a few suggestions to improve their duet. Then, as
Lakshmi left the stage, Ray approached her. "Hey, Lakshmi! Can I talk to you for a
second?" "Grr!" Ray laughed. "Rehearsal is over. You can stop being Sandy now." "Grr!" She
growled at him again and walked away. "But, Lakshmi—" "Attention, everyone!" Ms. Kwan clapped her
hands. "Before you leave, I have some good news. Parker will be back with us
onstage tomorrow. Isn't that right, Parker?" The kids yelled and applauded for Parker. He stood
up and bowed. "I'd also like to thank Ray for taking Parker's place these past
few days." This time not a single cast member clapped. Ms. Kwan looked puzzled. "I know
it's late and you're all tired, but—" "Come on, everybody," said Mr. Stein. "A round
of applause for Ray." There was some weak applause. Mr. Stein looked at Ms. Kwan
and shrugged. By now Ray was rushing toward the exit. "How's Parker doing?" Mrs. Aguilera
asked as Ray and Kyla got into their car. "Everybody's happy that he's coming back
tomorrow," Kyla said. "So, Ray, did you have a good time filling in for Parker?"
"Nope," Ray muttered. "Everybody hates him," Kyla said. Ray shot her a look. Why couldn't she
keep quiet? "What? Explain, please." Mrs. Aguilera turned toward Ray in the backseat. "It's horrible
being the villain in real life," Ray said. "I don't want to talk about it."
Parker returned to the stage. As the weeks passed, Ray started noticing that something was wrong with
Parker. Ray didn't see it all the time, and he couldn't put his finger on what it
was. But something was definitely off. Ray couldn't ask Parker because Parker still wasn't speaking to
him. Neither was Lakshmi. She continued to bark and growl whenever he tried to talk to her.
One day after they'd finished a scene, Ms. Kwan was talking to the cast. "Officer Ward, pat
Sandy on the head when you let her out of the box." The director turned her attention
to the other actors. "Annie, you need to . . ." Lakshmi was sitting at Ray's feet,
so he decided to pat her head. She snarled and tried to bite him. "Ouch! Did
you just snap at me?" he hissed at her. "Grr," Lakshmi growled. Kyla laughed out loud. "Serves
you right, Ray!" Ms. Kwan turned around. Ray expected her to yell at them for talking. Instead
she smiled. "Ray and Lakshmi, I'm proud of how hard you've been working as understudies." "If only
she knew," Kyla murmured. Ms. Kwan went on. "So, as a reward, you'll get to perform the
lead roles at the Saturday matinee!" "Oh!" Lakshmi jumped up. "That's exciting!" "Wow!" Ray was so
surprised, he couldn't say anything more. He'd given up any hope of playing Warbucks during an actual
performance. After he'd tried to sabotage Parker, he wasn't sure he even deserved the role. "Now you'll
have to shave your head!" Ben crowed. He punched Ray in the arm. "I can't wait to
see how that turns out." Ray faked a grin. He'd decided against a bald cap, but he
wished Parker and he could shave their heads together. No way was that happening now. That
night at home Ray pulled out his cast list. He had managed to convince Ben and a
few other people that he wasn't responsible for Parker's accident. They were talking to him. He put
a check next to their names. He put an X next to those who still thought everything
was his fault. Ray had no idea which side Kyla was on. Sometimes she seemed disappointed in
him. But one time he'd overheard her defending him to her friends. He put a question
mark next to her name. Ray looked at the list. There were a lot of X s.
*** The set crew finished painting the scenery. The actors' costumes were ready to be tried on.
Ray shaved his head. Two Saturdays in a row, the whole cast practiced from ten in the
morning until after dark. Tech rehearsals started with the light and sound crews. Opening night was coming
soon. For the final dress rehearsal, Ray was wearing his policeman's uniform. He liked the costume,
and he'd grown to like the part too. At the start of the play, he was sort
of a villain. But by the end, he was one of the good guys. The part wasn't
the lead, but it was fun to play. Ray sat in the cafeteria, where the actors waited
until they had to go backstage. To pass the time, he was playing cards with Ben and
some kids in the ensemble. "Hurry up and shuffle, Ben," Ray said. "I'm in the next scene.
This is a run-through, so Ms. Kwan won't be stopping for anything." "Unless there's an emergency,"
Ben said. He dealt the cards. "I wish we could see what's happening onstage. My cousin says
at his school they have a screen in the cafeteria. That way the actors can watch the
show." "That'd be nice," Ray said as he organized the cards in his hand. Suddenly an assistant
stage manager rushed into the cafeteria. "Ray!" she said breathlessly. "Ms. Kwan needs you right now." Ray
looked at the clock on the wall. "Already? They did that scene really fast." "No, they
haven't even started yet," said the stage manager. "Parker didn't show up!" "Okay, that's my definition of
an emergency!" Ben said. Ray dropped his cards on the table and pushed back his chair. "What?
Where is he?" The stage manager shrugged. "No one knows. Ms. Kwan couldn't reach him by phone.
You're supposed to change costumes and be ready to go on as Warbucks. Where's David? He has
to take your place as Officer Ward." "Hey, dude, this is your big chance," Ben said
to Ray. "Break a leg!" "Yeah, thanks," Ray said in an absentminded way. He was thinking of
other things. Such as: "What's wrong with Parker? Am I going to get the blame?" Ray changed
costumes and stayed in Ms. Kwan's classroom, which served as the boys' dressing room. With the door
open, he could hear the music from the auditorium. By paying attention to the songs, he'd know
when to go backstage. Something about putting on Warbucks' costume made Ray feel nervous. "Calm down,"
he said to himself. "You know this part. You know the nerves will pass as soon as
you get onstage." He paused as something suddenly occurred to him. "Ohh! Maybe that's it!" Ray found
his own clothes and pulled his phone from his jeans pocket. He texted Parker and waited a
few minutes. No response. He texted again. Nothing. "Come on!" he said. "I have to go onstage
in a minute!" But Parker still didn't respond. Ray heard Warbucks' servants singing. "That's my cue!"
And he ran backstage. *** The rehearsal went quickly. At the end of the curtain call, Ms.
Kwan signaled for the cast to remain onstage. "That was a good run-through! Thank you, Ray and
David for stepping in. Parker had better have a good excuse for missing this rehearsal. Otherwise, Ray
will be Warbucks in all the performances." She turned to Mr. Stein. "I told you we needed
understudies!" Mr. Stein nodded in agreement. *** After changing out of their costumes, Ray and Kyla
waited for their ride home. Ray scrolled through his messages. He was disappointed to see that there
was nothing from Parker. "I guess you're happy now that you might be Warbucks," Kyla said. "Not
really." Ray was busy texting Parker again. He looked up as their mother pulled in front of
the school. "I need Mom to drop me off at Parker's right away. I think he's in
trouble." Kyla nodded. "Yeah, it sounds like Ms. Kwan's really mad at him." "No, I'm talking
about Parker himself. Something's wrong with him." Kyla sighed as she slung her backpack over her shoulder.
"Did you do something else to him?" Ray shook his head. "No, he did it to himself!"
Ray found Parker lying on the couch, watching a soccer game on TV. "What are
you doing here?" Parker said. "Get out." "No, what are you doing here, Parker? Nobody misses
the final dress rehearsal—unless they're dead." Parker stared at the TV. "Goal!" shouted the announcer.
"Yes!" Parker pumped a fist. Ray moved right in front of Parker. "Look, I'm really sorry."
He swallowed hard. "I was trying to steal your part. I thought I deserved to
be Warbucks." Parker said nothing for a moment. "And . . . ?" "I'm sorry I
told you Ms. Kwan likes people to add lines." "Is that it?" "I shouldn't have
tried to confuse you about stage left and stage right. But I didn't leave that bucket
onstage. And I know what's wrong with you." Parker looked at Ray in surprise. "When
I put on the Warbucks costume today, I started feeling nervous. But I knew I'd
be okay as soon as I got onstage. That's what always happens. You're suffering from your
first case of stage fright," Ray said. "And you don't know how to deal with
it." Parker exhaled loudly. "The whole soccer team is coming on opening night. I don't mind
singing at rehearsals. But I can't sing to an auditorium full of people! Especially people
I know. My dad says to imagine the audience in their underwear. How can I do
that and remember my lines? I'm doomed!" "Tons of people watch you play soccer—" "Yeah,
but I've been playing soccer for years. This is my first show." "Look at it like
this." Ray pushed Parker's feet out of the way and sat down. "You never know
how a soccer game will end—no matter how much you practice. But you know how
a show will go because we've practiced every minute of it. Stage fright is just part
of doing a show. Everybody gets it. Everybody gets over it." Ray wasn't sure about
that last part, but it sounded good. And Parker appeared to be thinking about what he'd
said. "Okay," Parker finally said. "But what if I forget a line? Or my voice
squeaks? Or my friends start laughing really hard? Or . . ." Ray put his head
in his hands and stayed like that as Parker went on about all the terrible
possibilities. Then suddenly Ray raised his head. "Can your brother give us a ride to school?"
"I guess so." Ray took out his phone. "Who are you calling?" Parker asked. "Kyla."
When she answered the phone, Ray asked her to text her friends. "Tell them to
go back to school right now. I'm calling an emergency rehearsal." "Does Ms. Kwan know about
this?" "No." "Why should I help you?" Kyla sounded suspicious of Ray. "It's not for
me—it's for the show. Come on, Kyla, please." And with that one word— please —Ray revealed
how desperate he was. "I'll do it," Kyla said, "but on one condition. You let
me—and all my friends—hang out with you at the cast party." "No way!" "Come on, Ray,
you need all the friends you can get right now." Ray was in a hurry.
"All right, fine, whatever. I'll text the rest of the cast." He ended the call and
slapped Parker on the leg. "Get up, Parker. The show must go on!" *** Back
in the auditorium, Ray was happy to see that most of the cast had shown
up. "Attention, everybody!" "You sound just like Ms. Kwan," Ben said. Ray ignored him. "I called
this rehearsal because Parker needs our help. We have to show him we've got his
back. Right?" "Right!" echoed the cast. "We've had so many practices that everybody knows every line
in this show. Right?" "Right!" "So let's show Parker that he has nothing to fear.
We'll run the last scene. Only I'll be Annie, and, Lakshmi, you'll be Warbucks." Everyone laughed
as Ray recast the show. Kyla played Drake, the butler, while Parker was Grace, Warbucks'
secretary. The orphans played Warbucks' servants, and the servants played the orphans. "Okay, everybody, take
it from the top." Everyone was in good spirits as they made their way through the
scene. Whenever someone stumbled, the others helped out. As they reached the end, Ray turned
to Parker. "And that's what'll happen if something goes wrong. If you can't remember a line,
somebody will prompt you. If someone messes up a line, just respond like you think
Warbucks would respond. You're not onstage by yourself. We're—" "A team," Parker said. "Exactly! We're a—"
"Hey, what are you kids doing on that stage?" A janitor hurried down the aisle.
"You shouldn't be here without a teacher." "We're just leaving." Ray motioned to the cast. "Time
to go, everyone!" "Thanks, dude," Parker said quietly. *** On opening night the show went
off without a hitch—except for one moment when Warbucks' secretary missed a line. Parker had
the next line. Ray held his breath while Parker stood there in silence. Parker looked at
Ray, who gave him a nod. "Very good, Grace," Parker said in a strong voice.
Then he went on with his lines. Ray exhaled. During the curtain call, the audience applauded
wildly. "Parker! Parker!" called his soccer teammates. Parker grinned and bowed. As the cast left
the stage, Ray punched Parker's arm. "Way to go! You're a star!" "So are you!" Parker
said. "Hey, everybody, before you go!" he called out to the cast backstage. "You know
this was my first show. And I just want to say I couldn't have done it
without you—and especially without Ray. He saved me." The cast clapped and cheered. "Parker! Ray!
Parker! Ray!" The two friends took a bow. Then Parker went in search of the
soccer team. Lakshmi patted Ray's back. "What you did for Parker was really nice—and clever too.
Maybe you should be a director." "He's bossy enough to be a director," Kyla said
as she and her friends surrounded them. Ray and Lakshmi laughed. "I promise not to growl
at you anymore!" Lakshmi walked away. Ray smiled, feeling better than he had in weeks.
He was happy with his role in the play, happy with his friends. Happy with everything—until
his little sister interrupted his thoughts. "We can't wait to hang out with you and
your friends at the cast party," Kyla said. Her friends nodded. Ray groaned. "Are you sure
I agreed to that?" "Of course, I'm sure." Kyla grinned. "I never forget a line!"
